intro: Zoom for agile coaches on Mac comes down to three jobs: running retros on Zoom Whiteboard, splitting the team with breakout rooms, and keeping the session on time. The Zoom desktop app handles all three, but a few settings decide whether they work on the day.

Basic meetings stop at 40 minutes. Check your session length against your plan before you schedule it.

blocks.text: Agile coaches run a different kind of Zoom meeting than most people. You run retros, sprint reviews, and coaching calls. You switch between a whiteboard, breakout rooms, a timer, and a notes doc in one hour. This guide covers the Zoom settings that matter for that work on a Mac, and the limits that catch coaches off guard.

A note on sources first. Zoom's support and product pages cover the features here, and industry reports give the wider context. None of them describes a coach's exact routine. Treat the workflows below as a starting point, and test them with one friendly teammate before a real session.
Open Zoom Whiteboard from inside the meeting

Zoom Whiteboard is the board for retro maps, idea walls, and sorting exercises. You open it from the in-meeting controls, not from a separate app. The Whiteboards button starts a new board or opens one you already made.

items: Join the meeting in the Zoom desktop app for Mac. Whiteboard needs the desktop app, not a browser tab.
In the in-meeting controls, click Whiteboards.
Choose New Whiteboard for a clean board. Choose Existing Whiteboards to reuse last sprint's map.
Pick a mode. Collaborating gives edit access to everyone. Presenting gives view access.
Open the board with one teammate for a short test before the real session starts.

blocks.text: If the Whiteboards button does not appear, an account admin has to enable the feature. Ask your admin before the session, not during it. Zoom's article states no plan requirement for in-meeting use, so the admin setting is the usual blocker.
Choose Collaborating or Presenting mode on purpose
The mode decides who can change the board. Most whiteboard mix-ups in a retro come from picking the wrong mode. Check it before you share the link or open the board to the whole room.

headers: What people in the meeting can do
rows: Reading back themes, showing a finished map
blocks.caption: Existing whiteboard modes in a Zoom meeting, per Zoom Support.

blocks.text: Here is a 60-minute retro with 12 people. Open the main board in Collaborating mode for the writing round. Then open a second board in Presenting mode for the readout. People can read the themes, but they cannot move the sticky notes while you talk.

You can share a board outside the meeting through contacts, a Zoom Chat channel, or email. Do that after the session, when the map is final. A draft shared too early invites people to edit work that is not ready.
Run breakout rooms without losing the room

Zoom's breakout rooms page says a host can split a meeting into up to 50 sessions. Rooms can be assigned automatically or manually. Pre-assignment can be turned on in settings. Rooms can close on a timer, and you can broadcast text and voice to every room at once.

items: Turn on pre-assignment in settings before the meeting. Then name each room's members ahead of time.
Use automatic assignment for quick pairs. Use manual assignment when two people should not sit in the same room.
Set a timer so rooms close on time. Post the closing time in the meeting chat too.
Use a broadcast for the last warning. One clear sentence is enough.

blocks.text: Take an 18-person retro. Three rooms of six keep the talk short and give each person room to speak. Eighteen divided by three is six. Pre-assign three rooms and name one facilitator per room in your notes. Then you watch three rooms, not eighteen faces.

The common mistake is building rooms during the meeting. People sit in a waiting screen while you drag names around. Pre-assign instead, while the room is still empty. The setup is quick, and the room starts with energy instead of silence.
Zoom's breakout rooms page does not list which plans include the feature. Check the Zoom pricing page for your plan before you build a whole session around breakouts.
Know the plan limits before a long session

Plan limits decide how long your session can run. Zoom's pricing page lists Basic with a 40-minute limit and 100 participants. Pro lists 30 hours per meeting and 100 participants. Business lists 300 participants.

blocks.caption: Zoom plan limits and listed prices from zoom.us/pricing.

blocks.text: Take a 90-minute retro on Basic. It ends 50 minutes early, and the timer does not wait for your team to finish the last sticky note. If you are stuck on Basic, split the session into two linked meetings of 40 minutes or less.

Coaches often compare monthly prices and skip the meeting limit. Read the limit first. A cheap plan that ends mid-retro costs you the session, and the cost of rebooking is higher than the plan difference.
Whiteboard storage, uploads and guest access

Storage is the next limit to plan around. Zoom's getting started article lists 1 GB per board for Whiteboard Plus users and 200 MB for everyone else. The maximum upload is 35 MB. The article does not mention templates, so build your retro layout by hand, or reuse a board you already made.

items: Board storage: 200 MB per board on most plans, 1 GB with Whiteboard Plus.
Upload size: 35 MB maximum per file.
Guests: people without a Zoom account cannot receive the board.
Versions: new and classic whiteboards cannot run together in one meeting.

blocks.text: Photos fill storage fast. Compress them before you paste them into the board. A client who needs the result should get a written summary from your notes doc or email.
Classic whiteboard and admin settings that block you

Some whiteboard problems are not yours to fix. An admin can turn classic whiteboard on or off for all users, for specific groups, or for single users. The control sits in the Meeting tab, under the In Meeting (Basic) section.

A group or account lock can grey out your toggle. You then cannot change the setting yourself. Ask the admin who owns the lock. Zoom's article gives no effective date or deprecation date for classic whiteboard, so do not assume the setting stays the same.
Coaches who run sessions across several client accounts hit this most. A setting you see in one account may differ in the next. Check each account a week before the session, not the morning of it.
Keep your Zoom app current on Mac

Zoom's macOS release-notes page now points to one combined release-notes article for Zoom Workplace. Zoom says that article is the only one it will maintain. The notice lists no version or date, and third-party trackers disagree on the current Mac build. This page cannot tell you the current version, so check your own app.

Open the Zoom app, check for updates, and confirm the version in the app's About window before a big session. Menu names can change between releases. Trust the labels on your screen over any guide, including this one.
Ask Lazur for help without leaving the meeting

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud. It sees your screen only while you hold the keys, so you can ask in the middle of a retro without typing.

Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. Lazur does not click for you. It is not a plugin for Zoom, and it has no partnership with Zoom or any other app maker.
Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

For notes, hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Dictation is included and unlimited on both paid plans. Dictate the themes straight into your doc, not into a separate app.
A retro with Lazur, step by step

items: Before the call: ask Lazur to walk you through pre-assigning breakout rooms. Lazur waits for each click.
Start of the call: hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask where the Whiteboards button is. Lazur circles it.
Writing round: ask Lazur to set a timer for silent writing, so your eyes stay on the room.
Breakout: post the closing time in the chat, then broadcast the last warning.
Readout: switch to the Presenting board you prepared earlier.
After the call: hold fn and dictate the themes and action items into your doc.

blocks.text: Mistakes agile coaches make on Zoom Mac

items: Building breakout rooms during the meeting. Pre-assign them instead, while the room is still empty.
Opening the board in Presenting mode, then wondering why nobody can write. Check the mode before the call.
Planning a long session on Basic. The 40-minute limit ends the meeting, not the retro.
Sending a board link to a client without a Zoom account. They cannot receive the board.
Mixing new and classic whiteboards in one meeting. Pick one format for the whole session.
Leaving admin settings to the last minute. Ask the admin a week before, then test.

blocks.text: What the industry data says about remote retros

Microsoft's Work Trend Index (2025) reports that 57% of meetings are ad hoc calls without a calendar invite. Those figures come from Microsoft 365 telemetry across knowledge workers, not coaches. Expect more short-notice calls, so keep a saved board ready for them.

Digital.ai's 18th State of Agile report found that 74% of respondents use hybrid, blended, or homegrown Agile models. The survey drew nearly 350 people, mostly coaches and consultants from large enterprises. Smaller teams may look different.

The same release says 76% of respondents cite increased scrutiny on the business impact and ROI of Agile. Expect a sponsor to ask what your sessions changed. Keep a short written record after each retro so you can answer.
Set up your next session in this order

items: Check the session length and participant count against the Zoom pricing page.
Ask your admin to confirm whiteboards are on, and that the classic setting matches your account.
Pre-assign breakout rooms in settings while the room is still empty.
Create the board, pick the mode, and test it with one teammate.
Hold ⌥ ⌘ once and ask Lazur where the Whiteboards button is, so you know the shortcut works.

faq.question: Does Zoom Whiteboard work on a Mac?
faq.answer: Yes, through the Zoom desktop app for Mac. Zoom's article says Whiteboard needs the desktop app at or above the minimum version. If the Whiteboards button is missing, an account admin must enable it. Zoom states no plan requirement for in-meeting use.

faq.question: Can I use breakout rooms on the Basic plan?
faq.answer: Zoom's breakout rooms page does not say which plans include them. Check the Zoom pricing page for your plan before you run a session. Basic meetings also cap at 40 minutes, which limits how long the breakouts can run.

faq.question: How many breakout rooms can I create?
faq.answer: A host can split a meeting into up to 50 sessions, according to Zoom's breakout rooms page. Most retros need only a few rooms. Smaller rooms usually keep more people talking.

faq.question: Can a client without a Zoom account see the whiteboard?
faq.answer: No. Zoom says whiteboards cannot be sent to people without a Zoom account. Send them a written summary by email or from your notes doc after the session.

faq.question: Does Lazur watch my meeting all the time?
faq.answer: No. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: Can Lazur click buttons in Zoom for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points at things, answers out loud, and guides you one click at a time. It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It is not a plugin for Zoom.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur is a Mac app for macOS on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

faq.question: What does Lazur cost?
faq.answer: There is a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card. It starts when you first open the app. Pro is $18 a month, or $15 a month billed annually, with 250 AI actions. Dictation is unlimited on both paid plans.
